title: Ritual Purity and Communal Holiness
summary: A source-backed distinction between ritual impurity, moral offense, sanctuary access, and holy communal life in Leviticus.
historical_context: Leviticus assigns different causes, effects, remedies, and sanctions to bodily impurity and moral violations. Ritual impurity can arise without an act of personal wrongdoing.
ancient_near_east_context: Comparative ritual texts may clarify ancient concerns about sacred space and impurity, but Israelite categories must be derived from Leviticus's own terminology and structure.
literary_context: Leviticus 11-15 treats clean and unclean conditions, while Leviticus 18-20 addresses prohibited conduct and holy communal life; the sections are related but not interchangeable.
covenantal_significance: Purity instructions regulate life around God's dwelling and Israel's holiness, while moral commands govern covenant fidelity; later canonical reuse requires attention to changed contexts.
intertextuality: Leviticus 11-15 and 18-20 supply distinct contexts for later purity language in the Gospels and letters.

related_objects.notes: Primary literary setting for the distinction.

scripture_references.notes: Priestly examination of skin disease and garments.

interpretive_notes.note: Do not use 'unclean' as a synonym for personal guilt in every Levitical context.

common_questions: Does ritual impurity always mean personal sin?
How are purity and holiness related in Leviticus?

sources.title: The JPS Torah Commentary: Leviticus
sources.author: Baruch A. Levine
sources.notes: Jewish commentary integrating Hebrew text and modern scholarship.

claims.claim: Leviticus distinguishes ritual impurity from moral offenses rather than treating every unclean condition as personal sin.
claims.rationale: The sections describe different causes, consequences, remedies, and sanctions, although terminology and models remain debated.
